No single evaluated model (Allam, Falcon-H1, Qwen32, Silma) excels across all tasks, with best scores ranging from 0.516 F1 for localization to 0.880 Macro-F1 for detection, indicating distinct challenges per hallucination aspect.

deep_dive.overview: HalluTruthQA addresses the critical gap in Arabic hallucination evaluation by providing a comprehensive benchmark that goes beyond binary detection to include span-level localization, explanation, and factual verification. The dataset comprises 2,400 expert-curated QA pairs across Islamic knowledge, history, science, and geography, domains where factual precision is paramount. Each example contains a question, a model-generated answer, a verified reference, a binary hallucination label, erroneous spans, human explanations, and multiple-choice candidates for verification. The authors evaluate four open-source Arabic LLMs in zero-shot settings, revealing that hallucination detection, localization, verification, and explanation are distinct tasks with no single model dominating all. The taxonomy of hallucination types shows domain-specific error patterns, such as context inconsistency in Islamic knowledge and factual fabrication in geography. This fine-grained approach enables nuanced analysis of hallucination phenomena and supports the development of more trustworthy Arabic LLMs.

methodology.title: Dataset Construction
methodology.detail: 2,400 Arabic QA examples were expert-curated across four domains: Islamic knowledge, history, science, and geography. Each example includes a question, a model-generated answer from Fanar, a verified reference answer, and a binary hallucination label.

methodology.title: Multi-layer Annotation Scheme
methodology.detail: Annotations include character-level erroneous spans for hallucinated answers, human-written explanations describing the error, and six candidate answers for multiple-choice factual verification, enabling detection, localization, explanation, and verification tasks.

methodology.title: Evaluation Tasks
methodology.detail: Four tasks were defined: binary hallucination detection, span-level localization of errors, explanation generation evaluated by an LLM-as-a-judge protocol, and multiple-choice factual verification selecting the correct answer among six candidates.

methodology.title: Model Evaluation Protocol
methodology.detail: Four open-source Arabic LLMs (Allam, Falcon-H1, Qwen32, Silma) were evaluated in zero-shot settings on all tasks. Fanar-generated answers were used as input for hallucination assessment, with metrics including Macro-F1, F1-Sp, LO-Score, and explanation scores.

mechanism.title: Hallucination Taxonomy
mechanism.detail: Hallucinations are categorized into macro-types: Factual Contradiction, Context Inconsistency, Factual Fabrication, Nonsensical/Irrelevant Response, and Logical Inconsistency. This taxonomy guides annotation and analysis but no formal causal or geometric mechanism is provided.

experiments.title: Hallucination Detection
experiments.detail: Models predict binary hallucination labels on 2,400 QA pairs, achieving up to 0.880 Macro-F1, demonstrating strong but imperfect detection capability.

experiments.title: Span-level Localization
experiments.detail: For hallucinated answers, models localize erroneous spans at the character level, evaluated by F1-Sp score, with best performance at 0.516, indicating difficulty in precise error localization.

experiments.title: Explanation Evaluation
experiments.detail: Models generate explanations for hallucinated content, scored by an LLM-as-a-judge protocol normalized to [0,1], with best final score of 0.644, reflecting partial success in faithful explanation generation.

experiments.title: Multiple-Choice Factual Verification
experiments.detail: Models select the correct factual answer from six candidates, achieving up to 0.852 LO-Score, showing reasonable ability to identify correct facts among distractors.

findings.title: Domain-Specific Hallucination Patterns
findings.detail: Islamic knowledge exhibits high Context Inconsistency (61.6%) due to incorrect source attributions, while History and Science are dominated by Factual Contradictions (80.4% and 93.3%), highlighting domain-dependent hallucination characteristics.

findings.title: Task-Specific Model Performance
findings.detail: No single model excels across all hallucination tasks; for example, the best detection Macro-F1 is 0.880, but localization F1-Sp peaks at 0.516, indicating distinct challenges in detection versus precise error span identification.

findings.title: Explanation Evaluation Challenges
findings.detail: Explanation quality assessed via LLM-as-a-judge shows moderate scores (best 0.644), suggesting that generating faithful, complete explanations remains difficult for current Arabic LLMs.

findings.title: Factual Verification Effectiveness
findings.detail: Models achieve up to 0.852 LO-Score in multiple-choice factual verification, demonstrating capability to select correct answers among plausible alternatives, an important step beyond binary detection.

contributions: Introduction of HalluTruthQA, a fine-grained Arabic QA hallucination benchmark with 2,400 expert-curated examples across four knowledge-intensive domains.
Provision of a multi-layer annotation scheme including binary hallucination labels, character-level erroneous spans, human-written explanations, and multiple-choice factual verification candidates.
Comprehensive evaluation of four open-source Arabic LLMs on detection, localization, explanation, and verification tasks in zero-shot settings.
Development of a hallucination taxonomy highlighting domain-specific error types and motivating evaluation beyond binary detection.
limitations: Benchmark covers only four domains, excluding legal, medical, financial, or conversational Arabic QA contexts.
Answers are generated by a single LLM (Fanar), potentially limiting hallucination diversity and generalizability.
Span-level hallucination annotation is challenging due to implicit reasoning errors and boundary ambiguity despite expert validation.
Explanation evaluation relies on an LLM-as-a-judge protocol with limited human validation, which may introduce bias or inconsistency.
open_questions: How can hallucination evaluation be extended to cover additional Arabic QA domains such as legal or medical contexts?
What methods can improve span-level hallucination annotation accuracy, especially for implicit or attribution errors?
How can explanation generation and evaluation be enhanced to produce more faithful and comprehensive justifications for hallucinations?
Can integrating multiple LLM-generated answers increase hallucination pattern diversity and robustness of evaluation benchmarks?

papers.title: Capital Markets LLM Reliability Score (CM-LRS): From Plausible to Bankable
papers.abstract: In capital-markets workflows the question is rarely whether a large language model can produce a fluent draft, but whether the draft is bankable: defensible in front of a counter-party or a regulator, with the documents in hand. Existing methods address parts of that gap: open-domain QA benchmarks reward surface accuracy, and finance benchmarks (FinanceBench, FinQA, ConvFinQA) advance document-grounded and numerical QA but evaluate at the question-answer layer rather than the workflow outputs practitioners defend. We introduce CM-LRS, a Capital Markets LLM Reliability Score, evaluating outputs at the workflow-output layer across seven dimensions: factual accuracy, evidence traceability, numerical consistency, workflow completeness, source discipline, decision usefulness, and reviewability/auditability. Each is scored 0-5 against a rubric anchored on signals reviewers in regulated settings use; the aggregate is tunable to the workflow. We demonstrate CM-LRS on five workflows (DCM transaction-terms extraction, precedent retrieval, issuer profile synthesis, M&A transaction-comparable reasoning, ECM transaction-terms extraction) over public SEC EDGAR filings, a public UK takeover release, and fictional synthetic supplements, scoring four models against four independent LLM judges spanning three model families. Three findings. First, the frontier closed-source models cluster within 0.22 points on four-judge averaged CM-LRS (Sonnet 4.6 = 4.31, Opus 4.7 = 4.30, GPT-5.5 = 4.09); all four judges place the open-weights baseline (Llama 3.3 70B = 3.15) last. Second, that gap concentrates on retrieval (2.23) and synthesis (2.15), not extraction (0.84). Third, Decision Usefulness shows the widest cross-model dispersion of any dimension (4.0 points on issuer profiling) and top-tier inter-judge agreement (mean r = 0.52). Plausibility is cheap. Bankability is the bar.

deep_dive.overview: This paper addresses the critical gap in evaluating large language models (LLMs) for capital-markets workflows, where the key question is whether outputs are bankable—defensible and verifiable in regulated settings—rather than merely plausible or fluent. Existing benchmarks focus on question-answer accuracy but do not assess the full workflow output that practitioners must defend. CM-LRS introduces a seven-dimension rubric evaluating factual accuracy, evidence traceability, numerical consistency, workflow completeness, source discipline, decision usefulness, and reviewability/auditability, each scored 0–5 against rubrics grounded in real reviewer signals. The metric is demonstrated on five representative capital-markets workflows using public and synthetic data, scoring outputs from four models across three model families with four independent judges to control bias. Results show frontier closed-source models cluster closely in reliability scores, outperforming an open-weights baseline especially in retrieval and synthesis tasks. Decision Usefulness emerges as the most discriminative and reliable dimension for deployment readiness. CM-LRS thus provides a comprehensive, deployment-focused evaluation framework for trustworthy LLM use in regulated financial domains.

methodology.title: Seven-Dimension Rubric

methodology.detail: Unlike prior benchmarks that assess question-answer pairs, CM-LRS evaluates the entire workflow output, reflecting the actual deliverables bankers and analysts defend in front of regulators and counterparties.

methodology.title: Cross-Model and Cross-Judge Validation

methodology.title: Aggregate and Tunable Scoring
methodology.detail: Dimension scores are aggregated into a tunable composite CM-LRS score, allowing adaptation to specific workflow requirements and highlighting dimensions that require reviewer attention.

mechanism.title: No Explicit Mechanism or Equations Provided

experiments.title: Five Capital-Markets Workflows

experiments.title: Model and Judge Evaluation
experiments.detail: Outputs from four models (Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5.5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Llama 3.3 70B) are scored by four independent LLM judges from three model families, including in-panel and out-of-panel judges, to mitigate bias.

experiments.title: Dimension-Level Scoring and Justifications

findings.title: Frontier Models Cluster Closely

findings.detail: The open-weights Llama 3.3 70B baseline scores 3.15 on average, roughly one point below frontier models, with the largest performance gaps in retrieval (2.23 points) and synthesis (2.15 points) workflows.

findings.detail: Decision Usefulness (D6) shows the widest cross-model dispersion (up to 4.0 points on issuer profiling) and strong inter-judge agreement (mean Pearson r = 0.52), making it the clearest indicator of production readiness.

findings.title: Extraction Workflows Show Smaller Gaps

findings.title: Rubric Enables Rapid Review
findings.detail: The rubric’s per-dimension scores and justifications allow reviewers to quickly identify and verify specific claims, facilitating efficient auditability and reviewability.

papers.title: FlowCTS: On-policy Continuous Trajectory Supervision of Flow Models
papers.abstract: While on-policy distillation (OPD) effectively addresses sparse rewards and exposure bias in large language model post-training, its extension to flow models remains underexplored. To this end, we propose Flow Continuous Trajectory Supervision (FlowCTS), which matches subsequent student and reference trajectories initialized from the same student-visited state. Using the integral relation between trajectories and velocity fields, we derive a temporally weighted velocity-matching upper bound and discretize it into practical objectives parameterized by the number of supervision steps. Under a multi-reference setup, single-state FlowCTS-OPD outperforms vanilla KL-based OPD with faster convergence. FlowCTS-OPD improves GenEval from 0.90 to 0.93, OCR from 0.90 to 0.92, and PickScore from 22.75 to 23.06, while outperforming a mixed-reward RL baseline across all target metrics. Further analysis reveals a clear temporal supervision mismatch in vanilla KL-based OPD arising from its auxiliary SDE transition kernels. Beyond on-policy setting,FlowCTS also consistently outperforms vanilla SFT , particularly on OCR, while increasing supervision steps exhibit a trade-off between richer trajectory information and greater optimization difficulty.

summary.takeaway: FlowCTS introduces a continuous trajectory supervision objective for flow models that improves on-policy distillation performance and convergence speed over vanilla KL-based OPD.
summary.problem: Extending on-policy distillation to flow models is challenging due to their continuous velocity field parameterization lacking natural next-step conditional distributions.
summary.method: FlowCTS supervises the discrepancy between student and reference continuous trajectories from the same student-visited state using a temporally weighted velocity-matching upper bound discretized into multi-step objectives.
summary.evidence: FlowCTS-OPD improves GenEval from 0.90 to 0.93, OCR from 0.90 to 0.92, and PickScore from 22.75 to 23.06, converging faster than vanilla KL-based OPD and outperforming mixed-reward RL baselines.
summary.limitations: Increasing the number of supervision steps introduces a trade-off between richer trajectory information and greater optimization difficulty, with no consistent improvements observed.
summary.why_for_you: FlowCTS provides a novel dense supervision framework for flow models in on-policy distillation, addressing temporal supervision mismatch and offering a new scaling dimension relevant to LLM post-training.

signals.text: FlowCTS-OPD achieves balanced multi-objective performance, matching GenEval and OCR experts while retaining competitive PickScore, demonstrating the effectiveness of trajectory-derived supervision in multi-reference on-policy distillation.

The method derives a temporally weighted velocity-matching upper bound on continuous trajectory supervision, discretized into a finite number of steps parameterized by K, enabling both single-state and multi-step supervision in flow models.

Analysis reveals a temporal supervision mismatch in vanilla KL-based OPD caused by auxiliary SDE transition kernels, which FlowCTS overcomes by focusing supervision on early denoising stages where student-reference discrepancy is largest.

deep_dive.overview: This work addresses the challenge of applying on-policy distillation (OPD) to flow models, which differ from autoregressive language models by parameterizing continuous velocity fields without natural next-step conditionals. The authors propose Flow Continuous Trajectory Supervision (FlowCTS), which supervises the discrepancy between student and reference continuous trajectories initialized from the same student-visited state. By deriving a temporally weighted velocity-matching upper bound and discretizing it into practical objectives parameterized by supervision steps, FlowCTS enables dense trajectory supervision beyond token-level next-step objectives. Experiments demonstrate that FlowCTS-OPD outperforms vanilla KL-based OPD in convergence speed and multi-objective metrics (GenEval, OCR, PickScore), and also surpasses mixed-reward RL baselines. The method extends to off-policy supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with consistent gains, especially on OCR. The authors identify a temporal supervision mismatch in vanilla OPD due to auxiliary SDE kernels, which FlowCTS mitigates by focusing supervision on early denoising stages where discrepancies are largest. Increasing supervision steps introduces a trade-off between richer trajectory information and optimization difficulty, highlighting a new scaling dimension for flow models.

methodology.title: Flow Continuous Trajectory Supervision (FlowCTS)
methodology.detail: FlowCTS supervises the discrepancy between student and reference continuous trajectories starting from the same student-visited state. It derives a temporally weighted velocity-matching upper bound on the trajectory discrepancy and discretizes this into a finite number of optimization steps parameterized by K, covering single-state velocity matching and multi-step trajectory supervision.

methodology.title: On-policy Distillation with FlowCTS (FlowCTS-OPD)
methodology.detail: In the on-policy setting, the shared starting state is sampled from the current student rollout. FlowCTS-OPD applies the discretized trajectory supervision objective to improve convergence and performance over vanilla KL-based OPD by focusing on velocity matching along the trajectory.

methodology.title: Extension to Off-policy Supervised Fine-Tuning (FlowCTS-SFT)
methodology.detail: FlowCTS generalizes beyond on-policy distillation by allowing the shared starting state to be sampled from off-policy data trajectories, enabling supervised fine-tuning with the same trajectory-derived objective, which improves OCR performance while maintaining other metrics.

methodology.title: Temporal Supervision Analysis
methodology.detail: The method analyzes the temporal supervision mismatch in vanilla KL-based OPD caused by auxiliary SDE transition kernels that concentrate supervision in late denoising stages, whereas FlowCTS provides dense supervision in early stages where student-reference discrepancy is largest.

mechanism.title: Velocity-Matching Upper Bound
mechanism.detail: FlowCTS leverages the integral relation between continuous trajectories and velocity fields to derive a temporally weighted velocity-matching upper bound on the discrepancy between student and reference trajectories. This bound is discretized into practical objectives parameterized by the number of supervision steps K, enabling tractable optimization.

mechanism.title: Temporal Supervision Mismatch in KL-based OPD
mechanism.detail: Vanilla KL-based OPD constructs transition kernels via an auxiliary stochastic differential equation (SDE), which concentrates supervision in late denoising stages, causing a temporal mismatch with the student’s rollout distribution. FlowCTS addresses this by supervising the entire trajectory starting from the student-visited state.

experiments.title: On-policy Distillation Evaluation
experiments.detail: FlowCTS-OPD is evaluated on GenEval, OCR, and PickScore metrics using multi-reference Flow-GRPO models. It outperforms vanilla KL-based OPD, improving GenEval from 0.90 to 0.93, OCR from 0.90 to 0.92, and PickScore from 22.75 to 23.06, with faster convergence and better out-of-distribution generalization.

experiments.title: Off-policy Supervised Fine-Tuning Evaluation
experiments.detail: FlowCTS-SFT is tested with off-policy starting states, showing consistent improvements over vanilla supervised fine-tuning (SFT), particularly on OCR, while maintaining comparable GenEval and PickScore performance.

experiments.title: Training Budget Control Ablation
experiments.detail: A controlled study compares FlowCTS-OPD with K=1 and K=2 supervision steps, controlling for total supervised state evaluations. Results indicate that K=2 supervision yields better GenEval and compositional correctness, suggesting benefits from multi-step trajectory constraints beyond training budget effects.

experiments.title: Sampling Method Comparison
experiments.detail: Comparison of SDE and ODE sampling for generating student-visited states during on-policy distillation shows that SDE sampling consistently achieves higher GenEval performance, especially during early optimization.

findings.title: Improved Multi-objective Performance
findings.detail: FlowCTS-OPD achieves balanced performance across GenEval, OCR, and PickScore, matching expert models on GenEval and OCR while retaining competitive PickScore, demonstrating effective multi-reference trajectory supervision.

findings.title: Faster Convergence
findings.detail: FlowCTS-OPD converges faster than vanilla KL-based OPD across all three metrics, reaching expert-level performance substantially earlier, indicating the efficiency of the velocity-matching trajectory objective.

findings.title: Temporal Supervision Mismatch Identified
findings.detail: Vanilla KL-based OPD suffers from temporal supervision mismatch due to auxiliary SDE transition kernels focusing supervision on late denoising stages, whereas FlowCTS provides dense supervision in early stages where discrepancies are largest.

findings.title: Trade-off with Supervision Steps
findings.detail: Increasing the number of supervision steps K introduces a trade-off: richer trajectory information improves compositional and structural correctness but may suppress fine-grained details and increase optimization difficulty.

findings.title: Off-policy Gains on OCR
findings.detail: FlowCTS-SFT improves OCR performance over vanilla SFT while maintaining comparable GenEval and PickScore, validating the trajectory supervision formulation beyond on-policy distillation.

contributions: Proposed FlowCTS, a continuous trajectory supervision framework for flow models enabling dense on-policy distillation.
Derived a temporally weighted velocity-matching upper bound discretized into multi-step objectives parameterized by supervision steps.
Extended FlowCTS to both on-policy distillation and off-policy supervised fine-tuning settings with empirical validation.
Identified and addressed temporal supervision mismatch in vanilla KL-based OPD caused by auxiliary SDE transition kernels.
Introduced supervision step count as a new scaling dimension balancing trajectory information richness and optimization difficulty.
limitations: Increasing supervision steps does not consistently improve performance and introduces optimization challenges.
The trade-off between richer trajectory supervision and fine-grained detail preservation requires further exploration.
Temporal supervision mismatch analysis is limited to auxiliary SDE kernels; other flow model variants are not analyzed.
Evidence on generalization beyond evaluated datasets and tasks is not provided.
open_questions: How can the trade-off between supervision step count and optimization difficulty be better managed or mitigated?
Can FlowCTS be adapted or extended to other types of generative models beyond flow models?
What are the theoretical guarantees or bounds on convergence and generalization for FlowCTS in large-scale settings?
How does FlowCTS interact with different sampling methods or velocity field parameterizations in flow models?

papers.title: Simulating Tenant Responses to Energy Policy Interventions with Transaction-Cost-Aware LLM Age
papers.abstract: Recent studies use Large language models (LLMs) to simulate human opinions and decisions by prompting models with demographic, attitudinal, or persona-based descriptions. Yet such simulations rarely model the practical, cognitive, or social frictions that shape how people respond to policy interventions. Perceived transaction cost (PTC) provides a useful lens for modeling the practical frictions that shape policy responses, such as information burden, administrative effort, coordination demands, and perceived uncertainty. We use this lens to develop a friction-aware persona modeling approach for LLM-based simulation. In the context of energy-efficient renovation (EER), tenants are represented not only by who they are demographically, but by how they perceive the costs, benefits, barriers, and uncertainties associated with proposed renovation plans. Using survey data collected from 1,068 citizens in the Netherlands, comprising approximately 40,548 survey question and answer pairs, we compare prompt-only and fine-tuned settings across GPT-3.5-turbo, Ministral-8B-Instruct, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and evaluate supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) for local open-weight models. Results show that incorporating PTC-based personas and reasoning consistently improves model performance across both prompt-only and fine-tuned settings, suggesting that PTC-based persona design provides a useful bridge between institutional policy theory and interpretable LLM-based policy simulation. Code is available at https://github.com/xiaweijie1996/socialagent.

summary.takeaway: Incorporating perceived transaction cost (PTC)-based personas and reasoning into LLM simulations significantly improves the fidelity of tenant responses to energy-efficient renovation policies.
summary.problem: Current LLM-based simulations inadequately model the practical, cognitive, and social frictions influencing human responses to policy interventions, limiting their interpretability and accuracy.
summary.method: The authors develop a friction-aware persona modeling framework that integrates PTC-based personas and reasoning prompts into LLMs, comparing prompt-only and fine-tuned approaches across GPT-3.5-turbo, Ministral-8B-Instruct, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct models.
summary.evidence: Using a dataset of 1,068 Dutch citizens with 40,548 survey Q&A pairs, experiments show consistent performance improvements when PTC personas and reasoning are included, validated across prompt-only and fine-tuned settings with supervised fine-tuning and Group Relative Policy Optimization.
summary.limitations: The study focuses on energy-efficient renovation in Dutch social housing tenants, limiting generalizability; also, the paper does not provide detailed quantitative metrics for all model comparisons or address potential biases in LLM-generated responses.
summary.why_for_you: This work bridges institutional policy theory and LLM-based policy simulation by introducing a theoretically grounded, interpretable persona design that models practical frictions, advancing trustworthy and context-sensitive LLM applications in policy research.

signals.text: Incorporating PTC-based personas that capture perceived barriers and benefits such as financial sensitivity and immediate utility seeking improves LLM simulation fidelity in replicating tenant responses to energy policy.

The method uses a three-layer prompt design combining system instructions, PTC persona descriptions, and PTC reasoning prompts, alongside fine-tuning local open-weight models with QLoRA-based supervised fine-tuning and Group Relative Policy Optimization.

Experimental results on 40,548 survey question-answer pairs demonstrate that models with PTC persona and reasoning prompts achieve lower mean absolute error (MAE) in predicting tenant responses compared to demographic-only or no-PTC baselines.

deep_dive.overview: This paper addresses the gap in LLM-based policy simulation where existing models inadequately represent the practical frictions—such as information burden, administrative effort, and uncertainty—that influence human responses to energy policy interventions. The authors propose a novel persona modeling framework grounded in perceived transaction cost (PTC) theory, which enriches LLM prompts with personas reflecting tenants' perceived barriers and benefits related to energy-efficient renovation (EER). They implement a structured prompt design with system instructions, PTC persona descriptions, and reasoning checklists, and evaluate this approach on a large-scale Dutch survey dataset. The study compares prompt-only GPT-3.5-turbo baselines with fine-tuned local models (Ministral-8B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) using supervised fine-tuning and Group Relative Policy Optimization. Results consistently show that PTC-aware personas and reasoning improve model accuracy in simulating tenant responses, suggesting that this approach effectively bridges institutional policy theory and interpretable LLM simulation, thereby enhancing the trustworthiness and contextual relevance of LLMs in policy research.

methodology.title: PTC Persona Construction
methodology.detail: Tenant personas are constructed from survey indicators measuring perceived benefits (comfort, health, energy savings) and barriers (rent increases, disruption, distrust, uncertainty). These personas capture practical frictions and motivations relevant to energy-efficient renovation decisions.

methodology.title: Prompt Design
methodology.detail: Each survey instance is converted into a structured prompt with three layers: a system instruction to maintain persona consistency, a PTC persona prompt describing barrier- or benefit-oriented traits, and a PTC reasoning prompt that guides the model to reflect on burdens, uncertainties, and personal gains before answering.

methodology.title: Model Adaptation via QLoRA
methodology.detail: Local open-weight models (Ministral-8B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) are fine-tuned using QLoRA with 4-bit NF4 quantization and LoRA adapters. Two training regimes are used: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) learning directly from survey examples, and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) optimizing outputs with an explicit reward function.

methodology.title: Evaluation Setup
methodology.detail: Models are evaluated on a dataset of 1,068 Dutch citizens with 40,548 survey question-answer pairs, split into training (4,600 attitude-related pairs) and test sets. Performance is measured by mean absolute error (MAE) across benefit- and barrier-related questions under varying prompt and fine-tuning conditions.

mechanism.title: No Explicit Mechanism Provided
mechanism.detail: The paper does not present formal equations or causal models but relies on the theoretical framework of perceived transaction costs to represent practical frictions influencing policy responses, operationalized via persona prompts and reasoning checklists.

experiments.title: Prompt-Only Baseline Evaluation
experiments.detail: GPT-3.5-turbo is evaluated under three prompting conditions: no PTC information, PTC persona only, and PTC persona plus reasoning prompts, demonstrating incremental improvements in response accuracy.

experiments.title: Fine-Tuning Local Models
experiments.detail: Ministral-8B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct models are fine-tuned using QLoRA-based supervised fine-tuning and GRPO on 4,600 attitude-related survey pairs, with evaluation on the remaining data to assess gains from adaptation and PTC prompting.

experiments.title: Performance Metrics and Analysis
experiments.detail: Mean absolute error (MAE) is used to quantify prediction accuracy across survey questions, showing that models incorporating PTC personas and reasoning outperform demographic-only or no-PTC baselines consistently across benefit- and barrier-related questions.

findings.title: PTC Persona Improves Simulation Fidelity
findings.detail: Adding PTC persona prompts to GPT-3.5-turbo reduces MAE compared to demographic-only prompts, indicating better alignment with tenant responses influenced by perceived barriers and benefits.

findings.title: PTC Reasoning Further Enhances Performance
findings.detail: Including PTC reasoning prompts alongside personas yields additional accuracy gains, suggesting that explicit reflection on transaction costs aids LLM decision modeling.

findings.title: Fine-Tuning with SFT and GRPO Boosts Accuracy
findings.detail: QLoRA-based supervised fine-tuning and Group Relative Policy Optimization on local open-weight models further improve prediction accuracy beyond prompt-only baselines, validating the benefit of model adaptation.

findings.title: Consistent Gains Across Models and Settings
findings.detail: Performance improvements from PTC-based persona design and reasoning are observed across GPT-3.5-turbo, Ministral-8B-Instruct, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, demonstrating robustness of the approach.

contributions: Introduces a novel PTC-aware persona modeling framework for LLM-based simulation of policy responses.
Develops a structured prompt design combining system instructions, PTC persona descriptions, and reasoning prompts.
Demonstrates empirical improvements in simulating tenant responses to energy-efficient renovation policies using a large-scale Dutch survey dataset.
Evaluates and compares prompt-only and fine-tuned LLM settings including supervised fine-tuning and Group Relative Policy Optimization.
Bridges institutional policy theory and interpretable LLM simulation to enhance trustworthy AI applications in energy policy research.
limitations: Focus on Dutch social housing tenants limits generalizability to other populations or policy contexts.
Lack of detailed quantitative metrics for all model comparisons restricts comprehensive performance assessment.
Potential biases and variability in LLM-generated responses are acknowledged but not deeply analyzed.
No formal causal or mechanistic model is provided beyond theoretical framing of transaction costs.
open_questions: How well does the PTC-aware persona framework generalize to other policy domains and cultural contexts?
Can the approach be extended to model dynamic decision-making processes over time rather than static survey responses?
What are the best practices to mitigate biases and ensure fairness in LLM-based policy simulations conditioned on PTC personas?
How can explicit causal mechanisms linking transaction costs to policy responses be integrated into LLM simulation frameworks?

papers.title: LLM-SoccerArena: Benchmarking LLMs on Real-World Predictions in Sports
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support decisions about uncertain future events, yet evaluating their ability to forecast real-world outcomes remains difficult. In particular, existing benchmarks are typically static and retrospective, and therefore cannot test how information is synthesized by LLMs to predict future events under uncertainty. We introduce LLM-SoccerArena (https://llm-soccerarena.com), a prospective live benchmark that evaluates how well LLMs forecast real-world sports events before the outcomes are known. LLM-SoccerArena provides (1) a prospective live benchmark protocol, (2) a public open-source platform, and (3) a factorial benchmark design together with tournament-related questions (e.g., which team will win). LLM-SoccerArena automatically records timestamped, schema-validated forecasts of unresolved events, together with prompts, model versions, tool traces, and costs. The factorial design varies along four dimensions: (1) model version (e.g., GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8); (2) information access; (3) prompting strategy, and (4) forecast horizon. We demonstrate LLM-SoccerArena through a large-scale evaluation of the 2026 FIFA World Cup, in which seven LLMs generated forecasts for all 104 matches and 15 tournament-related questions. We provide a detailed analysis of model performance across information access, prompting strategy, and forecast horizon. As a result, LLM-SoccerArena provides new evidence about the forecasting performance of state-of-the-art LLMs. For example, LLMs with web access outperform those without, but only by a small margin (i.e., a 0.023 improvement in Brier score). Overall, LLM-SoccerArena provides a flexible, open-source platform for prospective benchmarking of unresolved events. LLM-SoccerArena will be continuously updated, and can be directly applied to future national and international tournaments and league competitions.

summary.takeaway: LLM-SoccerArena introduces a novel prospective benchmark for evaluating LLMs' forecasting abilities in sports.
summary.problem: Existing benchmarks for LLM forecasting are static and retrospective, failing to assess real-time predictive capabilities.
summary.method: The study employs a factorial design to evaluate LLMs across various dimensions, including model version and information access.
summary.evidence: In a large-scale evaluation of the 2026 FIFA World Cup, LLMs with web access showed a 0.023 improvement in Brier score over those without.
summary.limitations: The benchmark does not provide curated statistics or domain features beyond basic event information.
summary.why_for_you: This research is crucial for understanding how LLMs can be effectively utilized in real-world decision-making under uncertainty.

The benchmark protocol records timestamped forecasts, ensuring that predictions are made before outcomes are known, thus providing a genuine assessment of forecasting ability.

deep_dive.overview: LLM-SoccerArena addresses the challenge of evaluating LLMs' forecasting abilities by providing a prospective live benchmark that records predictions before outcomes are known. This benchmark is designed to overcome the limitations of static, retrospective evaluations by allowing LLMs to synthesize evolving information into probabilistic judgments. The study demonstrates its effectiveness through a large-scale evaluation of the 2026 FIFA World Cup, where it captures the performance of various LLMs under different conditions, revealing insights into their predictive capabilities and the impact of information access and prompting strategies.

methodology.title: Prospective Live Benchmark Protocol
methodology.detail: LLM-SoccerArena records timestamped forecasts for unresolved events, ensuring that predictions are made before outcomes are known, thus preventing artifacts from memorization.

methodology.title: Factorial Design
methodology.detail: The benchmark varies across four dimensions: model version (e.g., GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8), information access (web search vs. no web search), prompting strategy (scoreline vs. outcome probabilities), and forecast horizon (timing of predictions).

methodology.title: Evaluation Metrics
methodology.detail: Performance is assessed using accuracy and Brier score, allowing for a quantitative comparison of forecasting abilities across different LLMs and conditions.

methodology.title: Data Collection
methodology.detail: The benchmark automatically collects prompts, model versions, tool traces, and costs associated with each prediction, facilitating a comprehensive analysis of LLM performance.

mechanism.title: Information Synthesis
mechanism.detail: LLM-SoccerArena tests the ability of LLMs to synthesize evolving information into probabilistic judgments, reflecting their reasoning capabilities under uncertainty.

experiments.title: 2026 FIFA World Cup Evaluation
experiments.detail: Seven LLMs generated forecasts for all 104 matches and 15 tournament-related questions, allowing for a detailed analysis of model performance across various conditions.

experiments.title: Impact of Information Access
experiments.detail: The evaluation revealed that LLMs with web access outperformed those without, achieving a Brier score improvement of 0.023, indicating the importance of real-time information.

experiments.title: Prompting Strategies Analysis
experiments.detail: Different prompting strategies were tested, showing that direct score predictions led to varying levels of agreement between predicted scorelines and overall match outcomes.

findings.title: Performance of LLMs with Web Access
findings.detail: LLMs with web access achieved a Brier score improvement of 0.023 over those without, highlighting the advantage of real-time information.

findings.title: Effectiveness of Factorial Design
findings.detail: The factorial design allowed for systematic comparisons, revealing that different prompting strategies significantly influenced forecasting accuracy.

findings.title: Prospective Benchmarking Success
findings.detail: LLM-SoccerArena successfully recorded predictions before outcomes were known, providing a genuine assessment of LLM forecasting abilities.

contributions: Introduces a novel prospective live benchmark for evaluating LLM forecasting abilities in sports.
Provides a public open-source platform for continuous updates and evaluations.
Establishes a factorial design for systematic comparisons of LLM performance across various conditions.
limitations: The benchmark does not include curated statistics or domain features beyond basic event information.

open_questions: How can LLMs be further improved to enhance their forecasting accuracy in dynamic environments?
